title: The coal on the lips (Exodus Rabbah 1:26)
hook: baby Moses reaches for gold; an angel moves his hand to a coal, and his speech is slowed
tomorrow: who saw God more clearly than a prophet? not who you'd guess.

segments.voice: Yesterday: named by deeds, even God. Today, something done to a baby that marked him for the rest of his life.

Plenty of people wince at their own voice on a recording, or freeze when it's their turn to speak. Moses says it to God's face at the bush: "I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue." The man about to argue with Pharaoh is not a talker. The Torah doesn't say why. The midrash does.
screen: `FROZEN WHEN IT'S YOUR TURN.` → `I AM SLOW OF SPEECH.` → `WHY?`

segments.voice: Exodus Rabbah tells it. Baby Moses is growing up in Pharaoh's palace. He grabs Pharaoh's crown and puts it on his own head. The advisers panic: is this the one who'll take your kingdom? Test him, one says. Set gold in front of him, and a burning coal. If he reaches for the gold, he knows what he's doing. Moses reaches for the gold. The angel Gabriel pushes his hand to the coal. He puts it to his mouth, burns his tongue, and from that, the midrash says, came his slow speech. So: why is the messenger halting? The midrash's answer is that the limit came with being saved. The thing he'd later apologize for was the mark of the day he was protected. A neighbor tradition remembers Moses' tongue too. In the Qur'an, Moses asks: "And loose a knot from my tongue, That they may understand my saying." The same Moses, the same tongue, honored in both. And one honest difference. In Exodus, Moses pushes back, and God sends his brother Aaron to speak with him. In the Qur'an, Moses himself asks, for the knot to be loosed and for Aaron as a helper. Neither scripture tells the coal; that's the midrash's own gift.
screen: `I AM SLOW OF SPEECH.` · `GOLD, OR THE COAL?` · `THE LIMIT THAT CAME WITH SAVING.` · `LOOSE A KNOT FROM MY TONGUE.` · then, large: `THE COAL ON THE LIPS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let one limit of yours come to mind, something you'd change if you could: a stammer, a slow reading pace, a body that tires. Don't argue with it for now. Breathe with it, and wonder, for the length of the sit, what that limit has kept you from, or brought you to.
The coal on the lips: Exodus Rabbah's story of how Moses got his slow speech. A burn that came from being saved.
screen: `THE COAL ON THE LIPS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one: the coal on the lips, and the slow tongue still carried the message. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1581 COUNTS.` → `READING MIDRASH · 14 OF 40.` → `TOMORROW: WHO SAW GOD MORE CLEARLY THAN A PROPHET? NOT WHO YOU'D GUESS.`

howItsDone: The coal story from Exodus Rabbah is often told to Jewish children with the Torah portion Shemot; Moses, called Musa in Arabic, is honored as a prophet in Islam as well.

chat.meaning: In Exodus Moses says I am slow of speech, and he's still the one sent. A limit didn't stop the message.

Gabriel.meaning: an angel; in the midrash he moves baby Moses' hand

Pharaoh.meaning: Egypt's king, in whose palace Moses grows up

Aaron.meaning: Moses' brother, sent to speak with him

Exodus Rabbah.meaning: a collection of midrash on the book of Exodus

notes: Exodus Rabbah 1:26 paraphrased: the crown, the advisers (Balaam among them in the midrash; not named here), the test of gold and coal, Gabriel, the burned tongue. Confirm. Gentle for children: the coal is told without dwelling on injury.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Qur'an 20:27–28 in Pickthall 1930 as the neighbor tradition's own words. Confirm the exact Pickthall wording and capitalization. Honest difference: in Exodus Moses resists and Aaron is sent (4:13–16); in the Qur'an Moses himself asks for the knot to be loosed and for Aaron (20:29–32). 'Neither scripture tells the coal' refers to the Torah and the Qur'an; some Islamic commentary (tafsir) tells a similar coal story, which is not mentioned. Confirm with a Keeper of each path.
